title: Kialo -> Walton scheme annotation pilot

discussion.title: Should Governments Put A Tax On Meat?

conventions.confidence: how sure the annotator is that a careful human annotator would make the same choice (self-estimated)

scheme_fit.walton_or_book: walton.yml id or a scheme in Walton, Reed & Macagno 2008 (page given)

conventions.bindings: English uses the NASCQ templates on disk at annotation time, with bound phrases in ‘single quotes’ as on the WAG board; templates of proposed schemes are drafts
conventions.role_target: what the move really acts on, when that differs from the Kialo parent

selection.level_1: all 6 direct children of the thesis (3 pros, 3 cons: fewer than 6 of each exist)
selection.level_2: the direct children of 13292.7 (the most-voted con, 10 votes), 13292.13 (the con with the most diverse children) and 13292.118 (a pro whose children back and attack its premises): 5 + 5 + 3

items.text: Governments should put a tax on meat.

votes.scale: Kialo impact votes 0-4; vector = count per level

items.reading: A policy proposal put to deliberation: governments (unspecified, so read as any or all) ought to tax meat (rate, base and which meats unspecified). It is the claim at issue; it is not itself an argument.

scheme.id: n/a: claim at issue, statement should_be_performed(A)
scheme.source: the shared conclusion of AS:practical_reasoning and AS:consequences (core.yml should_be_performed/1)
typical_con_schemes: walton.yml negative_consequences (rebuttal; book p. 101), missing from WAG
answers to the pros' CQs: CQ:side_effect, CQ:other_means, CQ:best_means, CQ:possibility, and an efficacy CQ WAG lacks

alternatives.why_not: the claim names an action and an agent; 'should put a tax' is a practical ought

role.text: thesis (GameConfig.Claim)

bindings.conclusion_en: ‘tax meat’ should be done.
bindings.template_fit: Reads well, but the agent ('governments') is lost: WAG's schemes have no agent variable.

problems: Generic agent and no scope (which governments, which meats, what rate). Deeper claims argue the scope (tax only beef, exempt poor countries) as if they were pros or cons; they are really amendments of the action.
WAG schemes have no agent variable, so 'governments' disappears from the formula.

items.nascq_note: Nothing for the thesis itself. Its con side needs N1: WAG has no scheme that concludes ¬should_be_performed(A).

items.text: Taxes on meat would not resolve the problems associated with its production and consumption.

votes.scale: Kialo impact votes 0-4; vector = count per level

items.reading: Denies that a meat tax would achieve what its supporters want: the environmental and health problems of meat would remain. The claim gives no reason. It is aimed at the means-end premise that the pro arguments share ('taxing meat would lead to less meat being produced and eaten / would solve these problems').
implicit_premises: The pro arguments rely on the tax solving the problems of meat production and consumption.

alternatives.id: no scheme: a WAG question move on the efficacy premise of each pro
alternatives.why_not: the best model of a bare denial, but a question is not an argument, and AS:practical_reasoning has no efficacy CQ (N5)

alternatives.id: book p. 97 CQ5 'are other actions needed besides A?' (reading: the tax alone is not enough)
alternatives.why_not: the claim says the tax 'would not resolve' the problems, not that it is insufficient on its own

alternatives.id: NEW:ineffective_means ('A does not achieve G, so A should not be done')
alternatives.why_not: not a Walton scheme; it is the negation of a premise, not a new inference

role.text: answer to CQ:likelihood of the pros' scheme, attack, locus premise: brings_about({A},{G}) on AS:consequences (edge exists), would_bring_about({A},{S1},{S2}) on AS:practical_reasoning (edge missing, N5)
role.cq_source: book p. 102 CQ1 for consequences; for practical reasoning not in the five CQs of p. 96

alternatives.text: rebuttal of the thesis (enthymeme: 'a tax that does not solve the problems should not be imposed')

values.P1: a meat tax would not resolve the problems of meat production and consumption
values.C: ¬would_bring_about(tax meat, S1, less meat produced and eaten) of each pro

sentences_en: ‘a meat tax would not resolve the problems of meat production and consumption’
bindings.conclusion_en: Doing ‘tax meat’ in the situation ‘meat production and consumption harm the environment’ would not lead to ‘less meat is produced and eaten’.
bindings.template_fit: The negated template reads well, but the premise only restates the conclusion: as an argument it is circular, which is why a question move fits better.

problems: Bare assertion: no reason given.
Kialo attaches it to the thesis, but it targets a premise of each pro argument. One Kialo edge becomes several WAG moves, one per target argument.
'The problems' is vague: environment, health, animal welfare?
Its Kialo children do not support it as stated. 13292.174 is a side effect, 13292.104 is an 'other means' objection, 13292.145 is an amended proposal.

items.text: A [sin tax](https://www.investopedia.com/terms/s/sin_tax.asp) on meat would make food more expensive, despite many people not being able to afford it.

votes.scale: Kialo impact votes 0-4; vector = count per level

items.reading: A meat tax would raise food prices for people who already struggle to afford food. Making food less affordable for them is bad, so the tax should not be imposed.
implicit_premises: Meat is a significant part of the diet of people on low incomes.
Making food less affordable for the poor is a bad outcome (equity).

scheme.source: book p. 101, 'Argument from Negative Consequences'; walton.yml negative_consequences

alternatives.why_not: the claim states a consequence, not a value
only if N1 is rejected

role.text: rebuttal: an argument for ¬should_be_performed(tax meat)

alternatives.text: answer to CQ:side_effect of each pro, attack (exception side_effects({A},{S1}) on AS:practical_reasoning; conclusion locus on AS:consequences)

values.G: food becoming more expensive for people who already cannot afford it

sentences_en: Doing ‘tax meat’ brings about ‘food becoming more expensive for people who already cannot afford it’.
‘food becoming more expensive for people who already cannot afford it’ is bad.
bindings.conclusion_en: ‘tax meat’ should not be done.
bindings.template_fit: Reads well.

problems: The link only defines 'sin tax' (framing); it is not evidence.
'despite' is ungrammatical; read it as 'even though'.
'Food' overgeneralizes: the tax raises meat prices, not food prices in general. 13292.33 attacks exactly this.
The most-voted claim (10 votes, mean impact 2.2 on 0-4).

items.text: Meat production and consumption are bad for the environment.

votes.scale: Kialo impact votes 0-4; vector = count per level

items.reading: The claim only states the problem. The charitable completion: a tax would cut meat production and consumption, which would reduce environmental damage and promote environmental protection, so governments should tax meat.
implicit_premises: Taxing meat would lead to less meat being produced and eaten (S2).
Less meat production means less environmental damage (G).
Less environmental damage promotes environmental protection (V).

alternatives.why_not: the claim states a circumstance, not a consequence; the consequence would be wholly implicit
concludes about retaining a goal, not about an action; and walton.yml's version has a wrong conclusion

role.text: new pro argument for the parent

values.S1: meat production and consumption harm the environment
values.S2: less meat is produced and eaten

sentences_en: The current situation is ‘meat production and consumption harm the environment’.
Doing ‘tax meat’ in the situation ‘meat production and consumption harm the environment’ would lead to ‘less meat is produced and eaten’.
The goal ‘less environmental damage from meat’ would be achieved in ‘less meat is produced and eaten’.
Achieving ‘less environmental damage from meat’ would promote the value ‘environmental protection’.
bindings.conclusion_en: ‘tax meat’ should be done.
bindings.template_fit: Readable with the quotes. 'The current situation is <clause>' is clumsy, and 'achieved in <state>' is stilted.

problems: Only S1 is stated. Three of the four premises and the value are supplied by the annotator.
'Bad for the environment' is vague.
Its own children argue the premise S1, not the inference.

Higher prices reduce consumption.
Better health is good.

‘less unhealthy meat consumption’ is good.
bindings.conclusion_en: ‘tax meat’ should be done.

problems: 'Unhealthy meat consumption' presupposes S1, and it is ambiguous whether all meat consumption or only excess is meant.

items.nascq_note: None. If a con of this pro offers a better means, N10 is needed, because CQ:other_means is asked only of practical reasoning.

items.text: Taxing meat would raise the consumer price to reflect the real costs of meat consumption.

votes.scale: Kialo impact votes 0-4; vector = count per level

items.reading: The Pigouvian argument. Today's meat price leaves out costs borne by others (externalities, subsidies). A tax would raise the price to the real cost, and prices that reflect real costs are good (efficient, or fair: 'the polluter pays'). So tax.
implicit_premises: The consumer price of meat is below its real cost (S1; children 13292.11 and .218 argue this).
Prices that reflect real costs promote economic efficiency or fairness (V).

alternatives.id: AS:consequences (G = the consumer price reflects real costs)
alternatives.why_not: also fits the wording; practical reasoning was chosen because the claim names a target state, and its children argue S1
no value is named

role.text: new pro argument for the parent

values.S1: the price of meat is below its real cost
values.S2: a consumer price that reflects the real cost of meat

sentences_en: The current situation is ‘the price of meat is below its real cost’.
Doing ‘tax meat’ in the situation ‘the price of meat is below its real cost’ would lead to ‘a consumer price that reflects the real cost of meat’.
The goal ‘prices that reflect real costs’ would be achieved in ‘a consumer price that reflects the real cost of meat’.
Achieving ‘prices that reflect real costs’ would promote the value ‘economic efficiency’.
bindings.conclusion_en: ‘tax meat’ should be done.
bindings.template_fit: S2 and G nearly coincide: the template forces a split the claim does not make. V is a guess.

problems: The value is unstated and ambiguous: efficiency or fairness. That decides which value-based attacks apply.
S1 is implicit, yet two of its three children back exactly that premise. The annotator must make S1 explicit, or those children have nothing to attach to.

pattern_confidence_method: Per instance, joint = min(scheme confidence, role confidence): the chance that an annotator matches both if the two choices go together (an upper bound). roles_explained.new_pro: plain new argument for the parent
roles_explained.rebuttal: argument for the negation of the parent (or of the ancestor named in target)
roles_explained.cq_answer: answer to a CQ of a scheme (the parent's, or a sibling's when misplaced)
roles_explained.premise_backing: backs a premise of the parent directly
roles_explained.premise_attack: undermines a premise of the parent directly, with no CQ
roles_explained.none: no role of the vocabulary fits

mean_confidence.note: over the 19 arguments; the thesis is excluded. Self-estimated.

decide_per_pattern: P2 vs P3: one rule for the pros of a policy. Option 1: always AS:practical_reasoning. It keeps CQ:other_means, CQ:side_effect and CQ:possibility open to the con side, but needs two to four bindings the annotator invents. Option 2: AS:consequences when only a consequence is stated. Fewer invented premises, but no other-means question without N10. In this pilot the two were close for all three pros (0.55 vs 0.35, 0.5 vs 0.45, 0.55 vs 0.4).

P4: a con of a policy is a rebuttal by negative consequences (one Kialo edge, one argument, weighed against the pros), not an undercutter of every pro through CQ:side_effect. Recommended: the rebuttal. It matches Kialo's weighing of pros against cons, and WAG already gives CQ:side_effect a conclusion locus on AS:consequences.
P5: a bare denial of a premise becomes a question move (the proponent must then back the premise), not an Other argument whose premise restates its conclusion.

Misplacement (P11, P8, P5): may the WAG graph re-parent a claim, to the grandparent or to the sibling pros it really attacks? 5 of 19 arguments act on something other than their Kialo parent. If re-parenting is refused, they can only be Other arguments against the parent, which misstates them.

P13: may a child back a premise that the parent's annotator had to make explicit (S1 of 13292.118)? This requires the parent's bindings to be fixed before its children are annotated, and frozen afterwards.

Which NASCQ additions come first. N1-N4 (negative consequences, its CQs and backup edges) are needed by 8 of 19 arguments, as their own scheme or their parent's. N5 (the efficacy question) is needed by 3 more. N11 (comparative consequences) and N12 (an analogy change) each rest on a single instance: defer them.
decide_per_instance: The reading and its implicit premises: which consequence, which value (13292.118: efficiency or fairness?).
Which premise a child attacks when the text allows two: severity or likelihood (13292.25), efficacy or a better means (13292.169).
Whether a claim holds several arguments, and which one is primary.
Whether the Kialo relation fits the content, and if not, what the real target is.
How to phrase the bindings: A as a verb phrase ('tax meat'), states as clauses or noun phrases.
guidelines_must_say: The unit: one Kialo claim, read against its parent's formalization. Resolve anaphors ('this burden', 'this objective') from the parent. Say whether a claim's own children may disambiguate it (13292.169). Recommended: annotate the literal claim and record the child-informed reading as an alternative.

Implicit premises: list them, mark the bindings the annotator supplied, add only what the scheme needs, and never strengthen the claim. Here a mean of 0.74 bindings per argument (max 4) were supplied by the annotator.
Several arguments in one claim: one primary argument per item, the others as sub-items (e.g. 13292.36#2), because a WAG move is one argument.

Links: classify each as evidence (then a source-based sub-argument, usually AS:expert_opinion, for the premise it supports), as a definition or framing (ignore it), or as neither. Do not fetch links during annotation.
Record the role twice: relative to the Kialo parent, and relative to the real target (an ancestor, the sibling pros, a premise) when they differ.

Polarity: Kialo pro/con is relative to the parent's statement; WAG attack/defence is relative to the target argument. Under a con that is itself a premise attack, a Kialo con is a defence of that premise (13292.14, 13292.61). Work the polarity out; do not copy it.
Hedges ('could', 'might'): keep the scheme, and note the hedge as exposure to CQ:likelihood.

The role vocabulary needs more than the four roles of the brief. It needs 'undermines a premise of the parent directly (no CQ)', 'acts on an ancestor or on sibling arguments (misplaced)' and 'none' (amendments of the action).
The confidence scale: 0.8 or more when one scheme is obvious; about 0.5 when two are plausible; 0.3 or less when forced. These are self-estimates until double annotation measures agreement.
data_model_obstacles: Cons of the thesis against CQs of arguments. A Kialo con of the thesis that attacks a premise shared by all pros (13292.13) becomes one WAG move per pro argument (each needs target_arg_id), or a rebuttal that loses the premise it aims at.
WAG has no negative-consequences scheme, so the commonest con pattern can only be an Other argument today.

No scheme concludes that an outcome is good or bad (AS:values concludes 'a reason to keep a goal'). Backing or attacking good(G)/bad(G) (13292.25, 13292.36, one reading of 13292.180) is Other only. bad(G) is binary, so 'the burden is small' cannot be said.
The answer-variable binding breaks analogy between policies (13292.61): the proposition that held in the source case is not the answer's proposition (N12).
Practical reasoning's four premises force the annotator to invent S2, G and V when a claim states only S1 (13292.108), or to split one target state into S2 and G (13292.118).

No agent or scope variables, and no move that amends the action. 13292.145 (tax plus earmarked research), and the scope claims deeper in the tree (tax only beef, exempt poor countries), become new theses.
One argument per Kialo edge. A claim with two parents (13292.180) becomes two arguments with the same premises, and rule G1 (no restating) may reject the second.

Rule Q1: a bare 'there is a better way' (13292.169, best-means reading) cannot be a question, because an exception must be argued. It has to be an Other argument whose premise restates its conclusion.
Missing backup and ask edges: CQ:best_means has no backup scheme except the thesis-independent ones (N9), and CQ:other_means is asked only of practical reasoning (N10).

Bare claims carry their reasons in their own Kialo children (13292.13, 13292.169), but a WAG answer must carry its premises in the same move. So a Kialo claim plus its pros may be one WAG argument, not two.
process_recommendations: Before scaling, have a second annotator redo these 20 claims and about 30 more, and measure agreement on scheme and role separately. The confidences here are self-estimates.
The pattern inventory has not saturated: 15 patterns for 19 arguments, 10 of them single instances. Approve patterns in batches after every 20-30 claims, not once up front.
Annotate each discussion top-down and freeze a parent's bindings before annotating its children: a child's role depends on the parent's scheme and on its explicit premises.
Treat Other as a legitimate label. Here it is the honest primary label for 7 of 19 arguments, mostly bare denials and unargued factual or evaluative premises. That is not a failure of effort.
For bare claims, try 'claim plus its pro children' as the unit. The children are the premises of the claim's own WAG argument.
Select by centrality, not votes, below the first level: Kialo impact votes are sparse (median 1 per annotated argument, 5 with none).
